summary: We developed a website application, named “Ignova.” Our solution utilises NASA’s MODIS and VIIRS hot spots data to create an easy-to-use, useful, and interactive application. Ignova solves past issues with the separation of the previous MODIS data and new VIIRS data by harmonizing both datasets into one application. In the present, with the increasingly high global warming, many places (like the United Kingdom) are experiencing unusual climates. The unpredictability of the climate has harmed thousands of people and continues to do so. Our website application aims to assist users with identifying global heat patterns and heat anomalies using various visual graphs and statistics. The navigable website shows simple and complex graphs and statistics of user-selected regions (critical information for preparing against dangerous heat incidents). The Ignova application could help emergency responders distinguish and act upon abnormal heat incidents and natural heat incidents (using the alert notification feature and other features). The website application may also help data analysts in studying climate. For the majority of the public, the application simplifies complex information into simple summaries, predictions, graphs, and statistics, which can be used to prepare people, warn users of heat abnormalities, and potentially save lives.
details:
Ignova is a web app that gives emergency managers, scientists, and land managers one consistent record of burning activity for any area on Earth. NASA’s active-fire record is split across sensors that cannot be compared directly: MODIS (Terra and Aqua, 1 km pixels, 2000 onward) and VIIRS (Suomi NPP, 375 m pixels, 2012 onward). A user picks a preset region or draws an area on a MapLibre map. Ignova then returns a burning-activity calendar for that area, built from NASA FIRMS hotspots. The calendar shows fire seasons, the busiest months and years, and how the current month compares with the historical median, so the sensor of origin no longer matters.

How harmonization works: All detections are snapped to a common 1 km grid and counted as unique cell-days, so overpasses and pixel size do not inflate counts. VIIRS cell-days are then weighted by a ratio k, fitted per region and month so VIIRS totals match MODIS totals in the overlap years. Both sensors end up on one MODIS-equivalent scale, and the series does not jump when VIIRS joins in 2012. A Method tab shows the before-and-after blend, sensor agreement, and the fitted k values. We also document the known limit: later years may have a slightly higher detection floor.

Benefits and impact: Responders can see at a glance whether an area is unusually active, which periods of the year need monitoring, and how a current fire compares with past ones. They can also download the hotspots for their selection as CSV. The goal is faster early warning and better-informed fire response as MODIS reaches end of life and VIIRS takes over.

What makes it creative: Besides the calendar with an accessible red color ramp, Ignova has an Alerts page. Users save places or search an address, see live detections within 100 km with confidence percentages, and get phone notifications through ntfy.

Tools: Frontend in React 19, Vite, MapLibre GL, Tailwind CSS 4, Base UI, motion, and d3. Backend in Python with FastAPI, asyncpg, shapely, pyproj, and httpx, tested with pytest. Data in PostgreSQL/PostGIS on Supabase, fed by the NASA FIRMS API. Hosted on Vercel and Render, with Docker for local development and a daily near-real-time update job. We used a mix of Claude Code and Freebuff as AI coding assistants to speed up building the site.

Factors we considered: Audience (non-statisticians, so plain-language results), accessibility, fast demos (preset regions are preloaded, other areas are downloaded on demand and cached), API rate limits, and transparency about the method’s limits.
